summary: Light first shown in 1828 from Sherbrooke Tower, a Martello fort at the tip of Maugher Beach, McNabs Island; a concrete tower since 1941, boat access only.

structures.note: Sherbrooke Tower, begun 1814 or 1815 and completed 1828; the granite walls were demolished by about 1945, with ruins still standing in 1948 (NSLPS).

access.note: Reached by boat. Lighthouse Friends: grounds open, tower closed; the usual road to the light has washed out. A decent view from York Redoubt National Historic Site.

events.note: Sherbrooke Tower (a Martello tower) completed; work began 1814 (LF, NSLPS) or 1815 (Kinsman).
Lantern room on top of Sherbrooke Tower, in operation April 1828.
A third storey was added to the fort to house the light (Kinsman, section 10.2).
Abraham Gesner tests kerosene at the light. LF and NSLPS give 1851 (LF: permission in May 1851); Kinsman dates a month of government control under Gesner to December 1852.
Hurricane of 12 October 1871 seriously injured the tower; mortar cut out and repointed with cement.
Double row of piles driven along the beach for about 600 feet.
Neptune fog trumpet placed in operation 1 April 1889; fog bell moved to Georges Island.
Octagonal iron lantern room set on the tower; fifth-order Fresnel lens in place of lamps.
Fixed white changed to flashing white on or about 31 March 1903; dioptric fifth-order apparatus (Department report).
Ten-inch whistle replaced the reed horn as fog signal.
Tower raised ten feet; temporary light shown while the work was done.
Third-order Fresnel lens in a new lantern room; installed by 1906 (Department report).
New fog alarm building constructed; diaphone foghorn initially mounted on the lighthouse.
Diaphone moved from the lighthouse to the fog alarm building (inspection of 11 January 1907).
Double dwelling and boathouse built at the station.
New crib protection work; foundation of the tower protected by ballast covered with concrete (fiscal year ended 31 March 1922).
Winter storm tore much of the outer wall off the south side of the stone tower; the Martello tower was repaired.
HMS Revenge ran down and sank HMCS Ypres, a gate vessel tending the anti-submarine nets; no lives lost (NSLPS).
Present octagonal concrete tower built; replaced the 1828 light on the fort.
Demolition of the old granite walls of the Martello tower completed by 1945; substantial ruins remained as late as 1948.
Granite boulders added to the breakwater.
Fog alarm building demolished; foghorn moved to the lighthouse.
Full automation (Lighthouse Friends; NSLPS: automated by 1983).
Breakwater rebuilt with large granite boulders; the duplex house was razed and burned.
Foghorn silenced after sounding for 104 years.
Hurricane Juan breached the sand barrier between the ocean and the tidal pond; the lighthouse became harder to reach along the beach (NSLPS).

keepers.name: David George
keepers.note: Longest-serving keeper at the station (Lighthouse Friends); his careful kerosene records helped establish the fuel (NSLPS).

keepers.name: Edward Horne
keepers.note: Transferred from Peggy's Point; NSLPS roster spells him 'Horn, E.'. Salary raised to $450 in 1876 for the bell and to $500 in 1879 for an assistant.

keepers.name: William Iceton
keepers.note: Department keeper tables list 'Iceton, Wm.' for Mauger's Beach in 1906 ('Mauger Beach Light and Fog Alarm') and 'Wm. Iceton, sen.' in 1909. NSLPS spells him 'Iceton, W.'.

keepers.name: Hector G. Lowe
keepers.note: Lighthouse Friends: placed in charge in 1970, told in 1973 his job would end within six months, kept on until automation in 1983. NSLPS dates his hiring to 1973. Named here only in his public role, as the published sources give it.

wrecks.outcome: Norwegian bark lost control while tacking into the harbour and passed too close to the lighthouse, which took the wind out of her sails; crew scrambled ashore. Keepers displayed her signboard for years (NSLPS).
Gate vessel tending the anti-submarine nets, run down and sunk by HMS Revenge; no lives lost (NSLPS).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1941 (Wikidata) and 1828 (Rowlett) are both right for different structures. The first light (1828) was shown from Sherbrooke Tower, a Martello fort; the present concrete tower was built in 1941 and replaced it (NSLPS: '1941 - replaced original tower of 1828'). The register and Lighthouse Friends both give 1941 for the concrete tower.
The Register gives a "15 nautical mile range"; the Coast Guard list gives 10 nm. The story gives the Coast Guard figure as the current list value and states the Register's figure beside it.

corrections.why: NSLPS gives 'Owned by the Government of Canada'; Lighthouse Friends says the Canadian Coast Guard owns the light. The provincial figure appears to come from the island's status, not the light's.

corrections.current: McNabs and Lawlor Islands Provincial Park
corrections.why: The Coast Guard owns and staffs the light (Lighthouse Friends), and NSLPS gives federal ownership. The island's park status is a different fact about the land, not the light's agency.

notes_for_editor: Facts that rest on one secondary source: the early keeper dates (Bolser, McGlinn, George, Horne, Doody, Conrad) are from Lighthouse Friends and NSLPS, which agree; the Marine keeper tables (1906, 1909) confirm only William Iceton, matched by position on the OCR line (scan p. 188 and scan p. 344; printed pages not confirmed). The 1906 keeper table and the 1909 table are names read off OCR rows; a human should check the page images. Disagreements left open in the story: (1) the Martello tower start date, 1814 (LF, NSLPS) against 1815 (Kinsman), and its length, 13 years (Kinsman) against 14 (NSLPS); (2) Gesner's kerosene test, May 1851 (LF, NSLPS) against December 1852 (Kinsman, who also quotes 'It is said'); (3) the 1809 mutiny, six men executed at Halifax on 1 August (LF) against four men executed on 18 September (Kinsman); (4) Hector Lowe's hiring, 1970 (LF roster and LF text) against 1973 (NSLPS); (5) the present light, Iso W 4s (CCG list) against Flashing Yellow since 1992 (NSLPS); (6) range 10 nm (CCG) against 15 nm (register); (7) the island park status in the record (not verified from any source read; the story does not state it). The keeper years for Horne, Doody and Conrad are not confirmed by any Department of Marine passage read, so they rest on Lighthouse Friends and NSLPS. Chronicling America searches (Maugher, McNabs Island with lighthouse, 1860 to 1935) returned nothing usable. Storm and wreck items come from NSLPS and Lighthouse Friends (the 1872 and 1940 events and the 2003 hurricane are not separately confirmed; NOAA's HURDAT2 was not checked). Kinsman's 1995 text is an official Nova Scotia report hosted by the Friends of McNabs Island; the quotes used are short. The Register's 1941 date and its 'Second World War' upgrade sentence are used as the register's own words. Budget: about 9 page reads and 2 newspaper searches. The 1809 Columbine mutiny and gibbets are in the place section because they predate the light. Chapter count: the story has six chapters, each with sourced material, which is above the 2 to 4 chapter shape of a moderate story but within the rich shape. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1904 McNab Island entry (scan pp. 72-73, printed pp. 59-60) gives 31 March 1903 for the McNab light; the 31 March 1903 date in the Dartmouth entry is a different light. The 1906 keeper table (scan p. 344, printed p. 263) and the 1909 table (scan p. 188, printed p. 179) were read from the page images: "Iceton, Wm" at "Mauger Beach Light and Fog Alarm", appointed July 8, 1903, salary $800; and "Wm. Iceton, sen" at "Mauger's Beach Light and Front Light". The 1913 Department statement (scan p. 68, printed p. 61) also lists "W. Iceton, Sr." at Mauger beach with an appointment date of July 8, 1903 and a salary of $980; the story does not use it. Lighthouse Friends prints the contractor name as "Freemand and Griffin"; the story uses "Freeman" and this is not resolved. The 1906 detailed entry (scan p. 61, printed p. 54) and the 1907 summary (scan p. 23, printed p. 16) are both cited. The 1908 inspection entry (scan p. 54) records the 11 January 1907 inspection and does not state the day the diaphone was moved. The keeper years for Horne, Doody and Conrad are still from Lighthouse Friends and the Preservation Society only.
